name: PT Bank OCBC NISP Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank OCBC NISP: a wholesale franchise priced for a permanent shortfall
frontmatter.summary: Bank OCBC NISP is a wholesale-led Indonesian bank controlled by Singapore's OCBC, trading below the multiple its returns support. Loans are re-accelerating as surplus liquidity is deployed, but the margin is guided lower and credit costs are normalising; we model both. We initiate at BUY with a target well above the price and a dividend yield above the market. The main risk is a wholesale asset-quality cycle, and our bear case is a genuine loss of capital.
thesis: A mid-size, foreign-controlled Indonesian bank trading at a deep discount to the book value its returns support.
Loan growth has re-accelerated sharply as idle liquidity is redeployed; the margin is not recovering, and we model the company's own lower target rather than an expansion.
Through-cycle credit costs are covered by a capital ratio far above the regulatory floor and by loan-loss coverage above two hundred percent.

The controlling shareholder's stake caps the free float and limits index access, but the below-book multiple is explained by the return-on-equity gap against the cost of equity, not by the float, and we apply no separate float discount.
Payout sits at the policy floor while the bank rebuilds capital, and the step-up we model is a judgment the bear case removes entirely.
The genuine downside is a wholesale asset-quality cycle; our bear case prices a real capital loss, which is why we do not treat the discount as a floor.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Bank OCBC NISP with a BUY rating and a target price of Rp1,476, 28.3% above the Rp1,150 last traded and a total return of 32.3% once the 3.9% dividend yield is added. The stock changes hands at 0.5x our FY2026E book value and 5.1x FY2026E earnings, against a warranted multiple of 0.8x on a sustainable return on equity of 10.5% and a cost of equity of 12.5%. That gap is the whole call: the market is capitalising this bank as if its returns sat permanently below its cost of capital, and the operating record does not support that.

Three things move the value. First, the loan book is growing again after a stalled year: gross loans reached IDR190.80tn at the end of September 2026 against IDR173.37tn at the FY2025 close, and the loan-to-deposit ratio has recovered to 77.5% from 70.4% [S6, S2]. Second, the margin is not turning up with it: the company's reported net interest margin fell to 3.9% in FY2025 and management guides 3.7% for 2026, as time deposits grow faster than current and savings accounts [S2, S6]. We model the guided margin, not the redeployment hope. Third, credit costs are normalising from an unsustainably low base, and the balance sheet carries the loss absorption to meet it: a capital adequacy ratio of 23.7% and loan-loss coverage of 202.9% [S6].

What we are not underwriting is a re-rating to the multiples of the large state-linked banks. The free float is 14.0%, the controlling shareholder holds 85.1%, and the payout has been cut to the policy floor of 20.4% while the bank retains capital against double-digit loan growth [S0, S2, S8]. The float limits index access and makes the register dependent on one seller, which is a real reason a stock can trade away from fair value; it is not, however, the reason this one is cheap. The multiple is explained by the return on equity we model sitting a little under the cost of equity, and the call is that the price discounts a permanent shortfall well below even that: the warranted multiple we apply is below book, and the shares trade far below the warranted one. We do not apply a separate float or illiquidity discount because we cannot source its size, not because we think it is zero.

Bank OCBC NISP is a commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by OCBC Overseas Investment, which held 85.1% of the shares at the end of FY2025 [S2]. It describes itself as one of the ten largest Indonesian banks by total assets, loans and third-party funds, and it operates 202 offices across the country with 6,332 employees [S2]. The franchise is wholesale-led: at the FY2025 close, corporate, financial institutions, enterprise, commercial and emerging-business lending accounted for 83.9% of gross loans, with consumer banking taking the rest [S2].

The loan book is split by purpose rather than by product. Working-capital lending is the largest single use at just over two-fifths of the book, investment loans are a similar size, and consumption loans — dominated by mortgages — are the remainder; the working-capital and investment books grew in FY2025 while the consumption book shrank [S2]. On the funding side the bank runs a current-account and savings franchise that supplied 58.0% of deposits at the FY2025 close, with time deposits making up the balance [S2]. That mix is the bank's main structural advantage over the smaller private banks and its main vulnerability against the state-owned giants, which have deeper retail deposit pools.

The group relationship is the second defining feature. OCBC Bank of Singapore is the ultimate parent, and the Indonesian bank is run as part of a regional network rather than as a standalone domestic franchise: cross-border collaboration with the Singapore parent is an explicit strategic pillar, and the bank's wealth-management, private-banking and treasury products are built on the group's platform [S2]. The most important structural event of the recent past was the merger with PT Bank Commonwealth, whose integration the bank reports as complete; management credits it with expanding scale, broadening the retail and small-business customer base and adding wealth-management and automotive joint-financing capability [S2]. That transaction is the reason the FY2025 deposit book grew far faster than the loan book, and the reason the loan-to-deposit ratio had room to fall.

Revenue is still overwhelmingly interest income. On the audited face of the income statement, net interest income was IDR10.95tn in FY2025, down 0.9% from the year before, while other operating income reached IDR2.14tn, a 140.3% increase largely from gains on selling financial instruments and foreign-exchange transactions [S2]. The data pack reallocates roughly a trillion rupiah of that audited interest income into its non-interest line, so the pack's narrower net interest line prints IDR9.87tn and its non-interest line IDR3.22tn. After the reclassification, the franchise remains a spread business with a volatile trading overlay. Fee income proper — wealth management, transaction banking, trade finance and bancassurance — is the part management is trying to grow, and the disclosed growth in wealth-management assets and transaction volumes is the evidence that it is working [S2, S4].

Indonesian commercial banks earn the bulk of their revenue from the spread between what they charge
borrowers and what they pay depositors, so the shape of the funding mix matters as much as the size
of the loan book. Current and savings accounts are cheap and sticky; time deposits are expensive and
rate-sensitive. A bank that funds itself with a high share of transaction deposits can defend its
margin when policy rates rise and can cut faster when they fall. The corollary is that a bank growing
its loan book faster than its cheap deposits must either pay up for term funding or run down its
holdings of government bonds and central-bank placements, and that trade-off is visible in the
loan-to-deposit ratio.

The industry backdrop is one of slower but still positive credit growth. Bank Indonesia's survey of bank lending, published in October 2026, projects loan growth of 8.2% for the end of 2026, an upgrade on the prior survey but below the 9.7% actually delivered in 2025 [S7]. The same survey points to working-capital lending as the priority segment for new lending in the fourth quarter, ahead of investment and consumption loans, and reports a firmer new-lending sentiment indicator than in the third quarter [S7]. For a wholesale-led bank that is the right segment mix, and it is consistent with the acceleration NISP has already reported.

The rate environment is the dominant swing factor for margins. The house macro deck has the policy rate at 5.8%, inflation at 3.3% and real growth at 5.3% [S0]. A stable policy rate is a double-edged setting for a bank in NISP's position: it caps the repricing benefit on the asset side while deposit competition keeps the cost of funds sticky, which is why we model a margin at the company's own lower guide rather than one that recovers to its prior peak. The currency is the other external variable, with the rupiah at 18,004 against the dollar and the deck carrying 18,350 for next year [S0]; a weaker rupiah raises imported inflation and keeps Bank Indonesia cautious, which in turn limits how far deposit costs can fall. The desk's stance is explicit: the enabling regime is balance-of-payments pressure and CAUTIOUS, and Indonesian rate-sensitive banks' margins are carried on AVOID [S0]. This bank is not exempt from that; it is why the base case takes NIM down to the guided level, and why a deposit-cost squeeze is the bear case's second shock.

Competition is stratified. The large state-linked and systemically important banks dominate low-cost deposits and mortgage distribution; the large private banks compete on digital retail franchises; and the mid-size private and foreign-controlled banks, which is where NISP sits, compete on corporate relationships, trade finance and wealth management. NISP's disclosed position among the ten largest banks by assets, loans and deposits is the relevant marker of scale [S2]. Its edge is relationship depth in the corporate and commercial segments and access to the OCBC group's cross-border network; its disadvantage is a deposit franchise that is smaller and more expensive than the leaders', and a loan book concentrated in the segment where a domestic demand slowdown shows up first.

The competitive position is best read through the funding and capital numbers rather than through market-share estimates. A loan-to-deposit ratio of 77.5% at the end of September 2026, against 70.4% at the FY2025 close, says the bank has been lending into a deposit base it had built up rather than chasing deposits to fund loans [S6, S2]. A capital adequacy ratio of 23.7% says it can keep doing so without a capital raise [S6]. Those two facts are why we are comfortable modelling above-industry loan growth for a year without assuming the bank takes unpriced risk: it is deploying liquidity it already holds, not buying market share with price.

The moat, such as it is, is narrow and relationship-based. Switching costs in corporate cash management and trade finance are real but not absolute; the group network is an advantage for companies with Singapore or Greater China exposure but not for purely domestic ones; and the brand does not carry the deposit-pricing power of the largest banks [S2]. We therefore treat the franchise as one that can earn a return on equity around the cost of equity through a cycle, not one that deserves a premium multiple. That view is embedded in the valuation: our warranted multiple is below book, and the investment case rests on the gap between that and the price, not on a franchise re-rating.

The desk's sector caution has to be reconciled, not waved away. The same-week kill of PNBN.JK was driven by a bank earning a return on equity at roughly half its cost of equity, trading above the multiple its returns warranted, with a weaker CASA franchise and a rising provisioning trend against an improving headline NPL. NISP fails each of those tests in the safer direction: it earns a return close to its cost of equity, it trades below its warranted multiple, its CASA ratio and its coverage ratio are materially higher, and its loan-at-risk ratio improved to 4.8% [S2, S6]. The caution is still in our numbers rather than in the prose: we take NIM to the company's own lower guide, hold credit cost at the cycle average, and put the margin squeeze and the provisioning turn in the bear case together [S6].

The Indonesian banking market is unusually concentrated for an emerging economy, with a handful of
large banks holding most of the system's assets and deposits, and a long tail of smaller
institutions. Supervision is intrusive by regional standards: capital, liquidity and asset-quality
ratios are monitored quarterly, lending to related parties is capped, and single-borrower limits
constrain concentration. Foreign ownership of listed banks is permitted but subject to approval, and
several mid-size banks are controlled by regional banking groups that use them as the domestic arm of
a cross-border franchise. That structure explains why mid-size banks often trade below the book value
of their equity even when they are profitable: the free float is small, the controlling shareholder's
intentions set the dividend, and index funds cannot build a position.

The recent history is a story of a balance sheet that grew faster than its loan book. Gross loans rose from IDR170.46tn to IDR173.37tn in FY2025, a 1.7% increase that fell well short of the bank's own target range for the year, while third-party funds rose to IDR243.51tn [S2]. The consequence was a collapse in the loan-to-deposit ratio from 81.9% to 70.4% and a margin that fell to 3.9% from 4.4%, because the incremental deposits were parked in securities and placements rather than lent [S2]. On the data pack's narrower classification, net interest income fell to IDR9.87tn from IDR10.09tn, while non-interest income jumped on a trading and foreign-exchange gain; total operating income nonetheless reached IDR13.09tn and pre-tax profit IDR6.41tn [S2].

Costs were the offset. Operating expenses rose only modestly to IDR6.16tn, so the cost-to-income ratio on our definition fell to 47.1% [S2]. The reported efficiency ratio the bank publishes is a different measure and prints higher, at 69.6%, because it divides costs by gross interest and other operating income rather than by net operating income; we use the former throughout so that the ratio is comparable with the rest of our coverage [S2]. Impairment charges rose to IDR529.7bn from an unusually low IDR151.3bn the year before, which is the beginning of the normalisation we model [S2].

The nine-month figures show the turn. Net profit reached IDR4.03tn, up on the same period a year earlier, on loans of IDR190.80tn and deposits of IDR244.20tn [S6, S4, S10]. Total assets were IDR350.50tn [S6]. Asset quality is the one line that has moved the wrong way: gross non-performing loans are 2.0% against 1.6% at the FY2024 close, though the loan-at-risk ratio improved to 4.8% and coverage stands at 202.9% [S6, S2]. The funding mix also softened, with the CASA ratio at 55.1% against 58.0% at the FY2025 close, as time deposits grew faster than transaction accounts [S6, S2].

Our forecast takes the nine-month run-rate as the starting point rather than the annual plan. We model loan growth of 13.0% in FY2026E, which is the year-to-date expansion annualised, and deposit growth of only 2.7% because third-party funds were essentially flat against the FY2025 close at the end of September [S6]. That combination lifts the loan-to-deposit ratio to 78.3%. The margin is where we part company with the previous draft of this note: we model 3.3% on the engine's line, which is the company's own 3.7% 2026 target restated for the classification gap between the data pack and the audited accounts, not the 3.9% the bank reported for FY2025 [S2]. On the pack's line the FY2025 margin was 3.5%, so the base is a compression, not the expansion a flat reading would imply; on the company's definition it is the guided 3.7%, about a quarter of a point below the FY2025 print. Net interest income therefore rises to IDR10.13tn on the larger earning-asset base and total operating income to IDR13.41tn.

The company's own plan for 2026 is the anchor, and we follow it on the margin. It targets a net interest margin of 3.7%, a return on assets of 2.0% and a capital adequacy ratio of 21.0%, with loan growth of 8.0% to 11.0% and deposit growth of 10.0% to 12.0% [S2]. We are above the loan plan because the book reached IDR190.80tn at 30 September against IDR173.37tn at the FY2025 close, so the full-year plan is already met in nine months [S6, S2]; we are below the deposit plan because third-party funds were flat against the FY2025 close at the end of September [S6]. Where we agree is capital: the model's capital adequacy ratio starts at 23.8% in FY2026E and declines to 22.3% by FY2030E and 21.8% by FY2035E as risk-weighted assets grow faster than equity, still comfortably above the company's own target and the regulatory floor [S2, S6].

Credit cost is the assumption that carries the most weight. The audited sequence is a turn-year peak in FY2022, then 0.78% in FY2023, a trough of 0.09% in FY2024 and 0.31% in FY2025; the four-year average is 0.63% [S2]. We do not apply that average to the first forecast year. Nine months of 2026 are already reported: net profit of IDR4.03tn, up on the same period a year earlier, with coverage held at 202.9% and gross NPL at 2.0% [S6]. A full-year charge at the cycle average would have put the fourth quarter far below that delivered run-rate with no reported item to explain the drop, so FY2026E carries the charge the accounts are actually running at, 0.31% — the FY2025 print — and the normalisation to the four-year average starts in FY2027E at 0.63% [S2, S6]. From then on the charge is twice the last actual and at the cycle average, not below it, because the asset-quality measures are moving the wrong way: gross NPL rose from 1.6% at FY2024 to 1.9% at FY2025 and 2.0% at 30 September 2026, loan-at-risk is 4.8% and coverage 202.9% on a book that is 83.9% wholesale [S2, S6]. On that basis net profit is IDR5.16tn in FY2026E, a little above the IDR5.06tn of FY2025, a return on equity of 11.2%, and grows to IDR6.34tn by FY2030E as the loan book compounds and the cost base grows more slowly than income.

The model year opens below the last actual: the FY2026E return on equity of 11.2% compares with 12.0% in FY2025, a gap of about two-thirds of a point. The source is the margin guide — the company expects less margin in 2026 than it delivered in 2025, and we take the guide [S2, S6] — not the credit charge, which stays at the delivered level in the first year. The charge normalisation arrives a year later, which is why the FY2027E return on equity steps down to 10.1% when the four-year average takes over [S2]. A reader who compares the two years should read the opening year as the delivered run-rate and the following year as the normalised one, not as a forecast decline in the franchise.

Earnings quality deserves two flags. The first is the non-interest line: the FY2025 jump was a trading and foreign-exchange result, not a fee annuity, and we hold it broadly flat in FY2026E before growing it at a fee-led rate thereafter [S2]. The second is the provision base: FY2024 charges of IDR151.3bn on a book of IDR170.46tn were far below any through-cycle level, and the rebuild since then is the reason profit growth lags revenue growth in our forecast [S2]. Neither flag changes the direction of the call, but both mean the earnings base we capitalise is deliberately lower than the headline.

Capital allocation is straightforward. The bank pays a policy minimum of a fifth of earnings, having cut the FY2025 dividend to Rp45 a share, a payout of 20.4%, from Rp106 a share and a payout of half of earnings for FY2024 [S8, S9, S2]. The retained earnings fund loan growth of 13.0% against internal capital generation of roughly the return on equity times the retention ratio, which is why the payout stays at the floor for two years before stepping up as loan growth converges on the long-run rate. The step-up is modest against the payouts of the large covered banks, and deliberately so: this book is still deploying surplus liquidity, and the capital ratio falls rather than builds even with the higher payout, so the 30.0% payout is what the disclosed capital path supports. Book value per share rises from Rp1,911 to Rp2,461 over the explicit forecast, and the dividend per share from Rp46 to Rp60.

We value a bank on what its returns are worth against its cost of equity. The house method card names residual income as the engine and warranted price-to-book as the cross-check; the two are the same identity, because a constant-return bank is worth book value plus the present value of the spread over the cost of equity, and the closed form of that sum is the warranted multiple. The industry template carries warranted price-to-book as the primary at half the weight, residual income at three tenths and a dividend discount model at two tenths, and we keep that hierarchy rather than overriding it, because the two economically identical methods land about a tenth apart and the weighting choice does not drive the answer. The cost of equity is built from the ten-year government yield of 7.4% net of the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus a levered beta of 1.00 times the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives 12.5%, which is the ten-year yield plus an equity risk premium inside the band our method card sets for Indonesia. Debt carries no weight because this is a bank and deposits are not capital.

The primary method capitalises a sustainable return on equity of 10.5% against that cost of equity and terminal growth of 4.0%, giving a warranted multiple of 0.8x the opening book value per share and a value of Rp1,547 [S2, S6]. That return is the average of the three explicit forecast years; the terminal return the model carries into FY2035E is 10.0%, and the two differ by about half a point because the payout step-up and the loan-growth taper only partly offset each other. The label "sustainable" therefore means the through-cycle figure the forecast settles at, not the most favourable year inside it. If the terminal return is used in the same identity instead of the average, the warranted multiple falls by under a tenth and the value lands within a few per cent of the residual-income cross-check at Rp1,375, which is what one should expect from two forms of the same arithmetic.

The residual income method, which charges the cost of equity against book value year by year, lands at Rp1,375, -11.1% from the primary. The gap is about a tenth of the value and it is the honest measure of how little the method choice matters here: the question is the level of the return, not the algebra used to capitalise it.

The dividend discount model is the outlier, at Rp897, -42.0% from the primary. The divergence is arithmetic, not a signal about value, and the previous draft was wrong to call it structural. Two things drive it. First, the model distributes between a fifth and a third of earnings, so a dividend-only method capitalises only that fraction of the earnings the other two methods capture; the retained earnings accrue to book value and never enter the dividend stream. Second, the terminal growth of 4.0% is a nominal-GDP anchor, below the growth in dividends the explicit forecast carries at a constant payout and a terminal return near 10.0%; that fade is deliberate and it lowers the terminal value mechanically. The sign of the gap is therefore the sign one should expect from a low payout plus a fade to nominal GDP, not evidence that the bank is worth less than the other methods say. We keep it at its configured weight as a floor check on dividend capacity. With a payout at the level of the large state-linked banks the three methods would converge, and the bull case shows what that is worth.

The weighted value is Rp1,365 a share and the target, after the scenario weighting described in the next section, is Rp1,476. Two discounts are not applied, for different reasons. No liquidity discount is applied because the shares turn over IDR6,146.4m a day, which is enough for our position size [S0]. No float discount is applied either, but that is a limitation rather than a finding: the free float is 14.0% and the register is dominated by one holder, which limits index access and can widen a traded discount, and we have no sourced estimate of how wide. What the target carries is the return-on-equity gap: a bank earning below its cost of equity is worth below book, and that is the whole of the below-book multiple we apply. We would rather understate a discount we cannot measure than decorate the model with one. The target implies 28.3% of price upside and a total return of 32.3% with the dividend.

Two bridges are disclosed rather than applied. First, the valuation opens on the 30 September 2026 consolidated balance sheet [S0], the latest capital position the bank has reported, not on the audited FY2025 close: the equity it capitalises is about six per cent above the IDR43.86tn audited figure, and the price multiple quoted earlier is the multiple of the FY2025 audited book. Second, the engine converts consolidated equity into book value per share without deducting the minorities' share. The minority interest is small — parent equity is close to ninety-eight per cent of the consolidated figure — so the opening book value per share and the value it produces are overstated by under two per cent, a few tens of rupiah per share. Correcting it would lower the target by that amount, which does not change the call; we state it because the output contract is otherwise unbridged.

What today's price implies is the crux of the call. At Rp1,150 the shares trade at 0.6x the FY2025 book value, against a warranted 0.8x on the returns we model. Read through the same identity, the multiple at the price implies a sustainable return on equity of terminal growth plus that multiple times the spread between the cost of equity and that growth: 4.0% plus 0.6x times the gap between 12.5% and 4.0%. That is a return of roughly nine per cent, below the 10.5% we model and well below the 12.2% the bank reported for FY2025 [S2]. The market is therefore capitalising a permanent shortfall that the last three audited years do not support.

The engine's reverse-DCF output is worth quoting only to show why it is not usable. The solver perturbs the credit-cost input until the model reproduces the price, and it returns an implied credit cost of 28.9% — an absurd figure, because for a bank the value function is not monotonic in that input at these levels: the price sits below what any plausible credit cost produces, so the solver walks the input toward the edge of its bracket rather than to an economic answer [S2]. The price-to-book identity above is the honest version of the same question.

The first risk is asset quality in the wholesale book. Gross non-performing loans rose to 2.0% at the end of September 2026 from 1.6% at the FY2024 close, and although the loan-at-risk ratio improved to 4.8% and coverage is 202.9%, a book that is 83.9% wholesale is exposed to a domestic demand slowdown through a small number of large borrowers [S6, S2]. Our base case keeps the first forecast year at the delivered charge and then steps it up to the cycle average; the bear case takes it to the FY2022 level, which is the last time the cycle genuinely turned.

The second risk is funding. The CASA ratio fell to 55.1% from 58.0% as time deposits grew faster than transaction accounts, and the loan-to-deposit ratio is rising toward the low eighties [S6, S2]. If deposit competition intensifies while the policy rate stays at 5.8%, the margin compression we model is deeper than the guide and the cost of funds eats the benefit of the loan mix shift [S0]. This is the risk that most directly attacks the primary valuation method, because it moves the sustainable return on equity rather than a single year's earnings; it is the second shock in the bear case.

The third risk is the structure of the register. A 14.0% free float with a 85.1% controlling shareholder means the dividend is a board decision rather than a market expectation, index inclusion is limited, and a large seller can move the price [S0, S2]. That is a reason the shares can trade away from fair value and stay there; it is not the reason the multiple we apply is below book. The below-book multiple is the return-on-equity gap against the cost of equity, and we do not add a float discount on top of it because we cannot source its width. The honest position is that a permanent float-related discount would make the target lower than ours, not that our target already embeds one.

The fourth risk is execution and regulation. The Commonwealth integration is reported as complete, but mergers of this kind leave retention, systems and credit-culture risk in the years that follow [S2]. On the regulatory side, capital and liquidity requirements are being tightened across the system, and a bank with a 23.7% capital adequacy ratio has room but not unlimited room if risk-weighted assets grow faster than equity [S6]. A change to the dividend policy, positive or negative, would move the valuation more than any single quarter's earnings.

We weight the scenarios evenly around the base case, with the base at 50.0% and the bear and bull at 25.0% each. The shocks are set on the drivers that matter and anchored to history rather than to round numbers. The bear case takes credit cost to the FY2022 turn, the margin down through the company's guide on a deposit war, loan growth to the bottom of the plan, and the payout held at the policy floor instead of stepping up; it values the shares at Rp674, a substantial discount to today's price and not a floor: when the cost of risk and the margin move together the dividend does not protect the equity, because the payout is a fraction of an earnings stream that is itself falling. The bull case takes credit cost a notch below the base rather than back to the FY2024 trough — the trough is not a state we will underwrite as a bull while gross NPL sits at a five-year high — lifts the margin through the guide, takes loan growth to the current year-on-year rate and the payout to the level the capital ratio can fund; it values the shares at Rp2,248. We do not claim the shocks are arithmetically symmetric. The margin and growth shocks are mirrored around the base; the credit-cost shock is not, because the bear's headroom is the FY2022 turn while the bull's is bounded by the delivered first-year charge once the FY2024 trough is excluded [S2, S6]. The payout shock is deliberately asymmetric too, and the reason is structural: the stated policy is a minimum payout, so the bear cannot go below the floor without modelling a policy breach, while the bull's step-up is inside what the capital ratio supports [S2, S6].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A gross non-performing loan ratio that keeps rising for two consecutive quarters, a CASA ratio that keeps falling while the loan-to-deposit ratio rises, or a board that holds the dividend at the floor beyond the two years we model would each move us toward the bear case — the third is already in the bear's payout path, so seeing it would raise the bear's probability rather than change its value. A margin that holds through a policy-rate cut, or loan growth that stays in the mid-teens without a rise in credit costs, would move us toward the bull case.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. OCBC Overseas Investment held 85.1% of the shares at the end of FY2025 [S2]; the free float is 14.0% and institutions hold 88.7% of the register on the exchange's own record [S0]. The board is led by a president director who has run the bank through the Commonwealth integration, and the group appoints directors through the controlling stake [S6, S2]. There is no family control, no pyramid of holding companies and no dual-class structure; this is a subsidiary of a rated regional bank rather than a conglomerate, so the governance question is one of minority treatment rather than of related-party extraction.

Related-party exposure is small and disclosed. Loans to related parties were IDR128.1bn at the end of FY2025, a negligible share of a book of IDR173.37tn, and the group transactions disclosed in the accounts are banking services provided on commercial terms [S2]. We found no pledge of the controlling shareholder's shares, no enforcement action and no special notation on the listing in the record we reviewed [S2]. The audit is clean: the FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, a member of the PricewaterhouseCoopers network, with an unmodified opinion [S2].

The dividend record is the main minority-shareholder issue. The bank paid Rp106 a share for FY2024, a payout of half of earnings, and cut that to Rp45 a share, a payout of 20.4%, for FY2025, citing the need to strengthen capital [S8, S9, S2]. The stated policy is a minimum of a fifth of earnings with the meeting deciding the rest on capital needs, so the cut is within policy but it is a real transfer of value from income to growth, and it is why the dividend yield is not the reason to own the stock [S2].

On ESG, the disclosed position is a sustainable-financing portfolio of IDR36.20tn and a network of 202 offices [S2]. The material exposures for an Indonesian bank are governance and conduct rather than environmental: lending to carbon-intensive sectors, customer protection in wealth products, and data security. The bank reports sustainability financing and digital-service metrics but does not disclose a financed-emissions baseline in the material we reviewed, which is a gap rather than a red flag [S2].

The dated catalysts are the results calendar and the policy calendar. The FY2026 results, expected in late January on the pattern of the prior year's audit sign-off, will settle whether the fourth quarter delivered the loan growth the nine-month figures imply and whether the dividend stays at the policy floor [S2]. The annual meeting in April decides the dividend [S9]. Between those dates, each Bank Indonesia rate decision and the quarterly lending survey move the margin and growth assumptions that carry the valuation [S7].

The operating indicators we monitor between updates are the gross non-performing loan ratio, the loan-at-risk ratio and coverage, because together they tell us whether the credit-cost assumption is holding [S6]. On the funding side we track the CASA ratio and the loan-to-deposit ratio as a pair: a rising loan-to-deposit ratio funded by time deposits is the combination that erodes the margin [S6, S2]. On the earnings side we track the non-interest income line, because a repeat of the FY2025 trading gain would flatter profit without changing the sustainable return [S2]. And we track the capital adequacy ratio against the company's own target, because it is the constraint that sets the payout [S2].

bear.narrative: Asset quality turns: NPL gross rises through 2.5% as the wholesale book (83.9% of loans) meets a weaker domestic demand cycle, and with coverage held above 200% the credit cost that path produces is 1.33% — the FY2022 level, the last genuine turn. bull.narrative: The margin turn is stronger than modelled: redeploying the excess liquidity lifts NIM 40bp to 3.7% on our line (about 4.1% on the company's definition, still below the FY2024 4.39%) as CASA holds near 55%, credit cost improves a tenth of a point below the base in every year rather than returning to the FY2024 trough — the trough is not underwritten as a bull state while NPL sits at a five-year high of 2.0% and LAR is 4.8% — loans compound at 16% as the bank takes share in a market growing 8.2% (S7), and with CAR above the 21% target the board lifts the payout to 45%.
